label: lf-mogas
topic: Laia Mogas-Soldevila (UPenn Weitzman, DumoLab): biopolymer work and its overlap with green fire coatings and fire-test capacity
summary: Sources fetched 2026-11-13: profile page, dumolab.com, Crossref author query (filtered to her name), PubMed (5 records), arXiv (none). Her work is printed bio-based materials (chitosan, cellulose/wood biomass, silk, agarose, food-waste composites) with water-based fabrication, funded by Penn funds, NSF, J&J Foundation and ONR. Overlap with fire-retardant coatings is thin in the public record: the profile does not mention fire, and one 2026 conference abstract (Eggregate) reports surface charring as fire resistance in a cladding composite. Nothing public was found on the fire-test labor shortage; that comes only from Amit's seminar account.
lay_summary: Laia Mogas-Soldevila runs a design lab at the University of Pennsylvania that prints building materials from natural polymers such as chitosan, cellulose and silk, using water instead of harsh solvents.
Her chitosan prints fold themselves into shape as they dry, which is the same idea as the hygromorph bilayers in this track.
Her public papers barely mention fire; one 2026 abstract says a food-waste cladding resisted fire by charring.
We found nothing public about fire-regulation testing or a shortage of testers, so that link rests on what she said in the seminar.
Any fit with DELPHI is a hypothesis, and no one has been contacted.

recommendations: Treat the fire-coating fit as unverified; ask Amit for his seminar notes on what she actually said about fire regulations.
Read the full Eggregate paper to see what fire test was run and to what standard.
Read the ChitoFold chapter and RAMUS full text for chitosan or cellulose formulations that could be modelled as bilayers.
Source the actual fire test standards (for example ASTM E84, EN 13501) in a separate round; not done here.
